doc.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Hearing Charlie Parker with Charlie Shavers
summary: Shavers took him to hear a saxophonist in Harlem on a borrowed horn, and it changed his approach to jazz.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Now, was it when you were in the Dorsey band, you and Charlie Shavers, didn’t you kind of discover bebop around then? Didn’t you hear Charlie Parker for the first time with Charlie Shavers?

Yeah, it was, I think Charlie Shavers came, we ran into on Broadway sometime, and he said. “I heard this guy playing saxophone up in Harlem.” And he said, “I don’t know what he’s doing but it’s unbelievable. It’s fantastic stuff. He said, “I’m going to go up and listen to him the next couple of nights.” Or whatever it was. We had sometime off, so we went to hear bird. Strange, he was playing with a borrowed
saxophone, wasn’t even his. And he played this strange jazz, you know, for us it was kind of strange.
Do you remember where he was playing?

Nope. It might be Minton’s, but I’m not sure. But I could remember just thinking about how fantastic this was and he was, it kind of change my whole approach and whole thinking about jazz playing from that point on. It stayed with me; we went to see hear him a couple times after that, just absorbed what he was doing.
It had the same effect on Charlie Shavers?

Same effect on everybody, all of us, most of us, and especially Dodo Marmaroso. In fact, some weeks later, a month or whatever it was, Dodo said to me, “Why don’t you try to play clarinet like Charlie Parker plays the saxophone?” And I said, “Of course, I have that in mind, that’s what I want to do.” And I was fairly successful doing that.
